newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan govt panel mulls commodity market reforms.
newsitem.headline: Japan govt panel mulls commodity market reforms.

text.p: A Japanese government panel which met on Tuesday to discuss reform plans aimed at boosting the importance of local commodity futures markets is to make a detailed schedule in two years, a Trade Ministry official said.
The Commodity Exchange Council, an advisory body to the trade and farm ministers, proposed reforms including streamlining the process of introducing new contracts, he said.
"It took almost 10 years to launch aluminium futures in Japan. The council members agreed on the need for a more efficient procedure," the official said.

The Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) is to start trading the yen-based aluminium futures from April. TOCOM had to wait to obtain approval from the government for about 10 years, because of opposition from local aluminium end-users.
The council also discussed a more flexible way of setting commission fees in place of the current fixed system.
Trade house executives have cited high fixed commission rates as a key obstacle to expanding liquidity in Japan's commodity futures markets.
But the issue is highly sensitive in Japan as local commodity brokerages rely heavily on them for their livelihood.
"We understand local brokers heavily depend on revenue from commission fees. But a review of commission fees is needed to attract more money to markets," the ministry official said.
The council is also considering listing dollar-based commodity futures in Japan, he said. All commodity futures, including precious metals and grains, are at present yen-based.

Although Japan is a leading consumer of industrial commodities and grains, activity on its commodity futures markets has largely been limited to local speculators, while global prices are set on overseas exchanges.
